fixes.explanation: That's the number, friend. John 5:5 says this man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. That's a long stretch of years to live with that condition. Hold onto that number, because it makes what happens next hit even harder.

Twelve is a real stretch of time, but the text gives a much bigger number. The man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years (John 5:5). Twelve doesn't even get you to a third of that. So his condition had lasted far longer than you guessed.

That's it. He tells Jesus, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred.” (John 5:7). He adds that while he is on his way, someone else goes in before him. I think there's a lot of weight in that answer.

The man never mentions priests, and the text says nothing about anyone calling him unclean. His problem is simpler. He has no one to help him into the pool when the water is stirred, and while he is on his way, someone else goes in before him (John 5:7). That's all he says.

That's the word. He answers, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’” (John 5:11). His point is simple: the man who made him well is the one who told him to do it. That's the answer he gives the Jews.

Seeing belongs to the blind men in other stories. This man had been an invalid, and the one who healed him told him to pick up his mat and walk. So he says, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’” (John 5:11). The word is well.

Hearing isn't what happened to this man. He had been an invalid, and Jesus made him well. He tells the Jews, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’” (John 5:11). Well is the missing word.

Yes, friend. John 5:13 says the healed man did not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. He got healed, and the one who healed him was already gone. I think that's a head-scratcher, and I've never been so quietly vanished on.

The text doesn't report Jesus telling him to keep anything quiet. John 5:13 says the man did not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. So the reason the text gives is that Jesus was gone.

That's right. John 5:15 says the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. When they asked him earlier, he did not know who it was (John 5:12-13). Now he names Jesus to the Jews.

True! Jesus says, “…just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.” (John 5:21). Giving life to the dead is no small thing. That's a claim big enough to shake a chef's hat right off.

Life! Jesus says whoever hears His word and believes Him who sent Him “…has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.” (John 5:24). Crossed over, friend. Death on one side, life on the other.

Not just the good ones, friend. Jesus says “all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28-29). Then He says those who have done good go to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. The hearing isn't limited to the good ones.

Yes. Jesus says, “…My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.” (John 5:30). He also says, “I judge only as I hear.” So His judgment rests on the will of the One who sent Him, not on His own will.

That picture is from Psalm 1, where a person who delights in the law of the LORD is like a tree planted by streams of water (Psalm 1:2-3). Jesus doesn't use it for John. He says, “John was a lamp that burned and gave light…” (John 5:35). It's all about light here.

Signs from heaven aren't part of what Jesus says here. He says if someone else comes in his own name, they will receive him (John 5:43). That's the contrast. Jesus comes in His Father's name, and the other would come in his own.

The high priest isn't mentioned here. Jesus says, “…if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him.” (John 5:43). The key is the name. Jesus came in His Father's name, and this other one would come in his own.

Yes. Jesus says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one they trusted. And Jesus goes on to say that Moses wrote about Him.

Abraham, Israel's forefather (Isaiah 51:2), is a big name, but he's not the one Jesus names here. Jesus says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and the one they hoped in.

Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), but Jesus doesn't name him here. He says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one named. Jesus also says He Himself won't be the one accusing them.
